newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada serial killer presses case for release.
newsitem.headline: Canada serial killer presses case for release.

text.p: Canada's most notorious serial killer went to court on Tuesday to make a bid for freedom, fuelling calls for repeal of a law that allows murderers to seek early release.

Clifford Olson, self-described "Beast of British Columbia," is taking advantage of a section of Canada's criminal code that allows murderers serving life sentences to seek parole after 15 years in jail. Vilified across Canada, he was sentenced to life in prison in 1982 after pleading guilty to the brutal killing of eight girls and three boys in the Vancouver suburbs.

His effort began on Tuesday with a preliminary review of his application by the British Columbia Supreme Court. He took part by telephone from a maximum-security prison in Saskatchewan, where he is held in a special solitary confinement unit.

About 35 victims' relatives attended the hearing, which focused on procedural issues, and some family members appeared shaken as they listened to Olson, 54, argue before the court, at times reaching out to comfort one another.

He presented his own case, frequently using legal terminology and citing specific laws and precedents. He appeared well prepared although he rambled at times and displayed an uneven understanding of the law.

Citing concerns about the impact of publicity on potential jurors, Justice Richard Low prohibited the media from publishing details on the substance of Tuesday's session. He tentatively scheduled a full hearing on Olson's request for Aug. 18, when a jury will hear the case and Olson will attend.

Officials said Olson showed little sign he was rehabilitated and had virtually no chance of parole. They painted a chilling portrait of him, alleging he had sent pornography and threatening letters to victims' families and politicians from prison.
Olson seems to agree his chances are slim, saying in a letter to independent member of Parliament John Nunziata that "no jury in their right mind would grant me an early parole review."

But victims' relatives are angry that he has the right to ask for release after spending just 15 years in jail and the case has galvanised police groups, victims' rights advocates and some politicians to demand the law be changed.
"What is happening is immoral, unjust and unconscionable ... It is making a mockery of the justice system," Nunziata told an emotional news conference on Monday.

Added Brigitte Nordin, sister of one of Olson's victims: "How many more children have to die before they change the law? ... We want closure but obviously we will never have it because Clifford Olson sings and the government dances."

Called the "faint hope" clause, the law in question offers an exception to rules that deny murderers parole eligibility for 25 years. The clause was part of 1976 legislation that eliminated the death penalty in Canada and replaced it with mandatory life sentences for first- and second-degree murder.
The government in January revised the law so offenders no longer have an automatic right to seek early parole and multiple murderers were denied the right altogether.

But the changes were too late to affect Olson's case, and critics claim hundreds more offenders serving life sentences remain eligible for early parole review. They intend to make the law an issue in a federal election expected this year.
While expressing regret for the families' suffering, the government said it does not plan any more changes to the law.
